snip.t: Differential diagnosis: acute alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic gastritis, perforated or bleeding peptic ulcer, acute cholecystitis, acute appendicitis, mesenteric ischaemia, bowel obstruction, and inferior myocardial infarction.
snip.s: Internal Medicine (MBIM 4100) main exam, Paper One: 3 July 2019

snip.t: | Acute cholecystitis | RUQ pain, fever, Murphy’s sign, gallstones on US | Pain localized to RUQ, improves on leaning forward, gallbladder wall thickening without pancreatic enzyme rise |
Look‑alike conditions: duodenal ulcer perforation, biliary colic, mesenteric ischemia, acute cholecystitis.
Inspiratory arrest due to pain can support acute cholecystitis.
snip.s: Bedside Abdominal Examination: Ascites, Liver Span and Asterixis

snip.t: ❏ Acute cholecystitis:​ ​This can be successfully treated non-operatively but the high risk of recurrent attacks and\nthe low morbidity of surgery have made early laparoscopic cholecystectomy the treatment of choice.
